lessons.title: NBFCs, Insurers, and AMCs: Different Models Inside Financials

body.text: 'Financial services' on a factsheet can mean a bank, a gold loan company, a life insurer, a mutual fund house, or a stock exchange. They share a label and almost nothing else. A lender lives or dies by its cost of funds and bad loans, an insurer by the pricing of risk, and an AMC by market levels and investor flows. Analyse each with its own toolkit.

children.text: The last two lessons were about banks. But Indian financial services is far broader, and many of its fastest-growing listed companies are not banks at all: Bajaj Finance, Shriram Finance, HDFC Life, ICICI Lombard, HDFC AMC, CDSL, and BSE. This lesson gives you a map of the main business models and the one or two numbers that matter most for each.

markDefs.definition: A situation where a lender funds long-term loans with short-term borrowings. If the short-term money cannot be rolled over, the lender faces a liquidity crunch even if its loans are good.

children.text: An NBFC does the same basic job as a bank, lending money for a spread, but most NBFCs cannot raise current and savings account deposits. They borrow from banks, issue bonds and non-convertible debentures, and use commercial paper. That makes their cost of funds structurally higher, so successful NBFCs win by specialising where banks are weaker: used commercial vehicle loans, consumer durable finance at the point of sale, gold loans, or lending in smaller towns. Their big vulnerability is
. A bank's depositors rarely all leave at once; an NBFC's bond investors can simply refuse to refinance.

columns.label: Bank
points: Funded largely by deposits, including cheap CASA
Must hold CRR and SLR, which lowers yield on part of its assets

columns.label: NBFC

No CRR or SLR requirement, so more of its money is lent out
Depends on markets and banks staying willing to fund it
Specialised niches, often with higher yields and higher credit risk

body.title: What happened in the 2018 to 2019 NBFC crisis

children.text: In September 2018, IL&FS, a large infrastructure lender with top credit ratings, defaulted on its obligations. Mutual funds and banks, which had been buying NBFC commercial paper freely, suddenly pulled back from the whole sector. NBFCs and housing finance companies that had funded long-term loans with short-term paper found they could not roll over their borrowings. DHFL, a large housing finance company, later defaulted and went through insolvency. Well-run NBFCs with long-term funding survived, and some grew market share, but the episode permanently changed how investors analyse the sector. Since then, RBI has tightened NBFC regulation, including a scale-based framework that applies stricter, more bank-like rules to the largest NBFCs.

content.text: For NBFCs, check the asset-liability maturity profile in the annual report and the share of commercial paper in borrowings. A lender can have perfectly good loans and still fail if its funding disappears.

children.text: Life Insurers: Why Reported Profit Misleads

A life insurer spends heavily upfront on commissions, marketing, and setting up reserves when it sells a policy, but earns the profit over 10, 20, or 30 years of premiums. So the faster a life insurer grows, the more its reported accounting profit is depressed in the short term. This is called new business strain. That is why analysts largely ignore P/E for life insurers and focus instead on the value being created by new policies sold.

children.text: Product mix drives VNB margin. Pure protection term plans carry high margins. Non-participating savings products with guaranteed returns also tend to be profitable. Unit-linked policies (ULIPs) carry thinner margins because customers bear the investment risk and fees are capped. When stock markets boom, ULIP sales surge, so APE can grow fast while VNB margin falls. Also track persistency: the percentage of policies still paying premiums after 13 months and after 61 months. Low persistency destroys the future profits VNB assumes.

body.title: Budget Day for Life Insurers
body.scenario: In the Union Budget presented on 1 February 2023, the government announced that maturity proceeds from traditional life insurance policies (excluding ULIPs) would become taxable if the total annual premium on policies issued from 1 April 2023 exceeded ₹5 lakh. Until then, such proceeds were broadly tax-free. Listed life insurer stocks fell sharply on the day.
body.prompt: Why would this change hit insurer stocks so hard, and which metrics would you track over the next few quarters to judge the real damage?
body.modelAnswer: High-premium traditional savings policies, especially non-participating guaranteed-return products, had been sold heavily to wealthy customers as a tax-free, fixed-income alternative. These products carry good VNB margins, so losing the tax advantage threatened both sales volume and profitability. Insurers with a larger share of such high-ticket policies were most exposed. There was also a near-term effect: customers rushed to buy before the 1 April 2023 deadline, inflating sales in the January to March 2023 quarter and making the following quarters look weaker by comparison. Track: APE growth excluding the pre-deadline rush, the share of non-par savings in the product mix, VNB margin trend, growth in protection and annuity products that could replace lost volume, and management commentary on the average ticket size of policies.

markDefs.definition: Premiums collected by an insurer that have not yet been paid out as claims. The insurer invests this money and keeps the investment income in the meantime.

children.text: Motor, health, fire, and crop insurance policies are usually annual, so general insurers are judged on whether they priced risk correctly this year. The key number is the combined ratio: claims paid plus operating expenses and commissions, as a percentage of premiums earned. Below 100% means the insurer made an underwriting profit. Above 100% means it paid out more than it collected, but it can still be profitable overall by investing the
. The insurer's solvency ratio, which IRDAI requires to be at least 150%, tells you whether it has enough capital to absorb a bad year.

body.title: Calculate the Combined Ratio
body.prompt: A general insurer earns ₹20,000 crore of net premiums in a year. It pays ₹14,400 crore in claims and incurs ₹6,200 crore in commissions and operating expenses. What is its combined ratio? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Loss ratio = 14,400 ÷ 20,000 = 72%. Expense ratio = 6,200 ÷ 20,000 = 31%. Combined ratio = 72% + 31% = 103%. The insurer lost ₹600 crore on underwriting, so its overall profit depends entirely on investment income from the float. A combined ratio consistently near or below 100% signals disciplined pricing.

children.text: AMCs: A Toll on India's Savings Shift

An asset management company earns a fee as a percentage of the assets it manages. It needs almost no capital to grow, so listed AMCs tend to report very high return on equity. Revenue depends on two things the AMC only partly controls: the level of the stock and bond markets, and investor flows. Equity funds earn much higher fees than debt or liquid funds, so the equity share of AUM matters as much as total AUM. Steady SIP inflows, which crossed ₹25,000 crore a month for the first time in late 2024, give the industry a recurring, market-independent source of growth.

body.title: Illustrative AMC: AUM Mix Before a Market Fall (₹ crore)
What a Market Fall Does to AMC Revenue
body.prompt: The illustrative AMC above earns 0.60% a year on ₹4,80,000 crore of equity AUM and 0.25% on ₹3,20,000 crore of debt AUM, for annual revenue of ₹3,680 crore. Equity markets fall 15%, reducing equity AUM by the same percentage, while debt AUM is unchanged and there are no flows. What is its new annualised revenue, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: New equity AUM = ₹4,80,000 crore × 0.85 = ₹4,08,000 crore. Equity revenue = 4,08,000 × 0.60% = ₹2,448 crore. Debt revenue stays at 3,20,000 × 0.25% = ₹800 crore. Total = ₹3,248 crore, down 11.7%, even though not a single investor redeemed. Because costs are largely fixed, profit falls faster. AMCs are, in effect, a leveraged play on market levels.

body.title: Match the Metric to the Model
body.question: Which pairing of business and primary metric is correct?
body.explanation: VNB margin measures the profitability of new policies sold by a life insurer. CASA is a bank deposit metric, combined ratio belongs to general insurers, and persistency is a life insurance metric. Using the wrong metric for a business model is one of the most common mistakes in analysing financials.

body.text: Market infrastructure and broking stocks such as BSE, CDSL, and listed brokers are highly sensitive to trading volumes, especially in derivatives. Regulatory changes to F&O trading rules can reduce volumes quickly. Treat their boom-year earnings with the same caution as cyclical earnings.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: Because life insurers bear heavy upfront costs on new policies, analysts value them using Price to ___ Value rather than P/E.
body.explanation: Embedded Value captures net worth plus the present value of future profits from existing policies, which reported accounting profit does not reflect well.

body.title: Before You Buy Any Non-Bank Financial Stock
steps: Identify the business model: NBFC, life insurer, general insurer, AMC, or market infrastructure
For an NBFC, check cost of borrowings, funding mix, asset-liability maturity profile, GNPA, and capital adequacy
For a life insurer, check APE growth, VNB margin, product mix, persistency, and Price to Embedded Value
For a general insurer, check combined ratio over several years, solvency ratio, and concentration in any one product line
For an AMC, check equity share of AUM, fee yield trend, SIP flows, and market share
For exchanges, depositories, and brokers, check how much revenue depends on derivatives volumes and recent regulatory changes
Compare only with peers that share the same business model

points: Financial services includes very different models: banks, NBFCs, life insurers, general insurers, AMCs, and market infrastructure
NBFCs lend without cheap CASA deposits, specialise in niches, and are most vulnerable to funding shocks and asset-liability mismatch, as the 2018 to 2019 crisis showed
Life insurers' reported profit is depressed by new business strain; use APE, VNB margin, persistency, and Price to Embedded Value
General insurers are judged on the combined ratio; below 100% is an underwriting profit, and the float adds investment income
AMCs earn a percentage of AUM, so their revenue moves with markets and flows, with equity AUM earning the highest fees
Exchange, depository, and broker earnings depend heavily on trading volumes and regulation
